title: Set up your workspace and review a change
outcome: Deliver a small tested change with a readable history.
story: Amina wants a teammate to use your shipping fix. They need the files, the steps to run them, and a clear record of what changed.

frames.explanation: A branch separates the change from the main version.
Passing tests and a readable change make another person’s review possible.

sections.title: A folder, an editor, and a terminal
paragraphs: A project is a folder containing related files. An editor helps you read and change them. A terminal accepts commands that run programs or work with files. Run one command at a time and read its output before moving on.

Install Node.js and Git using their official downloads. In your terminal, node --version and git --version should print their versions. Open a new terminal after installing a tool if the old terminal cannot find it. Keep your work in a new learning folder, separate from other projects.

sections.title: Keep a history with Git
paragraphs: Git records versions of files. A repository is a folder with that history. A commit is a saved change with a message explaining its purpose. Git works locally; GitHub is a service where you can share a repository and review proposed changes.

Start with git init in your learning folder. Use git status to see changed files. Select the intended files with git add, then make a commit. Avoid adding everything blindly: look for private files, temporary output, and unrelated changes first.

sections.title: Review a small branch
paragraphs: A branch is a named line of work. Use git switch -c feature/shipping-fix to create a branch for the repair. A diff shows what changed between versions. Read it with git diff before committing.

A useful review explains the problem, resulting behaviour, and tests. Include the unpaid-order reproduction from lesson 6. The browser exercise below checks a release decision; it does not run Git. The project requires real commands and a real commit in your own workspace.

sections.title: Make the work reproducible
paragraphs: Another developer should be able to obtain the project and run its checks using the README. Record the runtime version, file names, command, and expected result. A clean second folder is a useful test of those instructions.

Keep API keys and other private configuration out of the repository. An .env.example can contain empty placeholders and descriptions. Filename checks are only one guard: a secret can appear inside any file, so review the contents of the diff too.

words.meaning: A project folder with a recorded change history.
A saved change and its explanation.
A view of the lines added or removed by a change.

explanation: The branch name describes the change.
testsPass records whether the checks succeeded.
Both conditions must hold before this simplified workflow proceeds. Real review also examines the diff.

exercise.title: A review-readiness rule
exercise.brief: Write assessChange(files, testsPass, branch). Return stop:tests, stop:main, stop:private, or ready. Check in that order. This is a planning exercise; complete the Git project on your computer.

steps.title: Stop after a failed check
steps.task: Return stop:tests when testsPass is false.
steps.hint: Check the result before considering the branch or files.

steps.title: Keep main separate
steps.task: Reject changes prepared directly on main or master. Use stop:main.
steps.hint: Check both protected names after checking the tests.

steps.title: Exclude private file names
steps.task: Reject .env files and .pem or .key files. A placeholder .env.example is allowed, but still needs content review.
steps.hint: Use files.some with a filename condition. The provided pattern also catches .env.local in a subfolder.

project.title: A reviewed shipping fix
project.brief: Create a real local Git repository containing your lesson 6 repair, its tests, and run instructions. Share a reviewable branch if you use GitHub.
deliverables: The repaired program and check command.
A feature branch with a focused commit.
A README and short review description.

milestones.title: Set up the folder
actions: Download and unzip the exercise kit into a new folder.
Run its check command and read the output.
Run node project-check-shipping.mjs; the supplied project file intentionally reproduces the bug.

milestones.title: Make the change
actions: Initialise Git and record a starting version.
Review git diff, stage the intended files, and commit.

milestones.title: Hand it to another person
actions: Record the commit id and check result.
Try the README in a clean second folder.
Write the problem, behaviour, and validation in the review description.

acceptance: The project runs using its README.
The repair is on a feature branch.
The diff contains only intended changes.
No real credentials or private files are committed.

tests.expected: The documented command runs the checks.
Only intended files and empty configuration placeholders.

project.extension: Ask someone to review the change and address one concrete piece of feedback. Record what changed and why.
reflection: What is the difference between Git and GitHub?
What did reviewing the diff reveal?
Which instruction made the project reproducible?

files.SHIPPING-START-HERE.md:
# The real Git project

The readiness planner is only the browser warm-up. Run `node project-check-shipping.mjs`: it deliberately fails against project-shipping.mjs. Reproduce the failure, initialize Git, commit the starting version, create feature/shipping-fix, and repair that file using lesson 6. Run the command again, inspect git diff, and make a focused commit. The reference file is a learning aid; explain your repair before using it. Record your branch, commit, check output, and clean-folder setup test.
